The space of binary matrices is vast, making it difficult to randomly sample a matrix from this space efficiently. One approach to overcome this challenge is to represent a binary matrix as the result of performing random operations on a row or column basis. Our research contributes a novel and efficient algorithm for sampling binary matrices at specific densities. The proposed method utilizes a 'degree-based' approach to ensure that sampled matrices maintain a specified level of non-zero entries. To accelerate sampling, we also developed a technique that pre-computes a binary matrix based on the desired density, reducing the associated sampling cost. The proposed algorithm exhibits a time complexity of O(n^2 log n), making it more efficient than previous methods. Additionally, our research extends the concept of sampling to fixed margin binarized matrices, which are matrices with specified marginal sum values. The proposed algorithm for sampling fixed margin binarized matrices involves a binary matrix conversion technique to ensure compliance with the specified marginal sums. Sampling fixed margin binarized matrices at specific densities is achieved through a 'degree-based' approach, and a technique called 'binary vector propagation' is introduced to enhance algorithm efficiency. The proposed fixed margin binarized matrix sampling algorithm exhibits a time complexity of O(n^3), but can be optimized to O(n^2 log n) when sufficient off-the-shelf binary matrix sampling is available.

We introduce a comprehensive open-source library, named \texttt{pdffit}, for fitting parton distribution functions and related calculations. Based on \texttt{nhlcxx}, the code is fully transparent and compatible with various input formats. Its flexibility allows users to define their own fit objectives using a range of available options or by implementing their own functionality via function pointers. Moreover, the code includes pre-defined templates for popular parton distribution functions and relevant evolution equations are provided by \texttt{nhlcxx}, ensuring the accuracy of results. A detailed guide is available in the accompanying documentation, enabling users to customize the code for their specific needs.

This document outlines the recent developments and enhancements incorporated in the 0.7.5 version of the ELKI data analysis platform. The underlying philosophy of the library adheres to the principle of incorporating a wide range of features from statistical pattern mining and unsupervised linear regression, catering to advanced users. The open-source framework is built upon Java, facilitating the development of efficient, scalable, and reliable algorithms. The process of maintaining and evolving the library involves a combination of automated testing and manual quality assurance procedures. The aim of this chapter is to provide an overview of the latest additions to the framework, which serves as a tool for conducting in-depth data analysis in various scientific fields.

We introduce a theory to initiate an optical frequency domain microresonator and explore its applications for generating multi-frequency arrays. By adjusting the pump power in a microresonator, it is possible to control the formation of solitons through its influence on the phase mismatch in a specific Kerr nonlinear medium. As a result, it becomes possible to initiate an optical frequency domain microresonator and generate an array of solitonic frequencies that can be used for applications in nonlinear optics and quantum comb engineering.

We establish a condition for a subgroup of an acylindrically hyperbolic group to be loyal, meaning that it excludes any virtual membership of its members in other discrete groups. In simpler terms, a subgroup is loyal if it doesn't virtually belong to another discrete group. We demonstrate that many prominent subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups meet this loyal criterion, including those that only contain the identity element, orientable surface groups, and groups generated by a single edge exchange. We also find that a loyal subgroup of an acylindrically hyperbolic group is itself non-virtual, meaning it has no membership in another discrete group.

Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats neural networks with binary weights as simple symmetric kernel methods and analyzes their Neural Tangent Kernel characteristics. It demonstrates that the kernel's smoothness or regularity varies directly with the bit length during the initial training stages. This regularity is the key to improving generalizability. Additionally, since the regularity is most pronounced in binary weight networks, these networks offer the best improvement in generalizability. However, this improvement comes at an additional cost, which is evaluated and estimated to be in the range of several percent.

In various quantum systems, researchers have discovered the entanglement pyramid - a thermal entropy structure that shares similarities with the geometry of space. For example, the entropy of smaller regions in a larger system follows a pyramid-shaped structure with respect to their shared border. By using holographic duality, we extend the understanding of this entanglement pyramid to higher dimensions, and reveal the presence of critical surfaces within the bulk. We observe that the entropy of smaller regions in the bulk is described by a pyramid-shaped structure with respect to their shared border, and that this pyramid exhibits an additional, deeper layer. We derive a general formula for the different layers of the entropy, and demonstrate that the entanglement pyramid is an inherent property of higher-dimensional entropy in both black holes and quantum critical surfaces.

When a solvable lattice framework undergoes a configuration change by moving a joint, the intersection multiplicity at that joint can be calculated using an algebraic approach that doesn't require further movement of the joint. This method has recently been proven to produce the same results as the "intersection multiplicity" concept introduced in molecular mechanics, without relying on the framework's geometric structure or the path of configuration change. This paper provides an algorithm to calculate the intersection multiplicity in solvable lattice frameworks using finitely many polynomial equations and confirms that the resulting multiplicity values are indeed integers. It also presents a method for calculating the multiplicity of a specific lattice framework structure, known as the "prismatic configuration", which has recently been applied in the modeling of proteins and nucleic acids.

Many iterative algorithms in the Compressed Sensing field exhibit slow or non-convergent behavior when solving sparse matrix inversion and related problems. To address this issue, researchers have employed various stabilization techniques derived from Newton-Kantorovich and quasi-Newton methods to accelerate convergence and achieve stable solutions. Our study provides an in-depth analysis of these stabilization approaches for iterative algorithms in Compressed Sensing.

We obtain a mathematical expression for the point spread function (PSF) of a difference image, which involves subtracting two or more astrophotographs taken at different focal lengths from a telescope observation. This difference technique is typically employed to reduce the impact of bright stars and improve the detection of extended objects in optical and infrared astronomy. Our PSF formula is applicable to situations where the detector sensitivity varies, which can occur due to non-uniform illumination, and our findings are confirmed through the use of numerical models. Additionally, we analyze the PSF structure in the context of a difference algorithm and propose a method for approximating the PSF based on the properties of a difference operator. Our work is relevant to the research of various astronomical phenomena, including the study of the Milky Way, Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays, and the structure of the Dark Matter halo.

In a recent study, we've identified multiple ways to link a subdomain of the complex plane, bounded by a contour following a stochastic path, with both a discrete set of random walk points and a associated field of statistical probability. These linkages, driven by a mathematical equation in the form of a complex value, are connected to several independent processes: one being similar to a mathematical equation used to predict probabilities, another related to a statistical field, and several independent processes following the mathematical equations used to predict probabilities for fractal geometries. By linking these components, we've established multiple independent relationships, each driving a different mathematical equation in the form of a complex value, to a set of statistical probability points distributed throughout the domain. These components, defined within a mathematical equation in the form of a complex value, are connected to a set of statistical probability points distributed throughout the domain. These components, driven by a mathematical equation in the form of a complex value, are related to several processes following the mathematical equations used to predict probabilities for fractal geometries.

This research explores the behavior of solutions to the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions with constant density, focusing on their growth rate as time approaches infinity. Unlike non-periodic conditions, where growth is governed by the Lyapunov exponents, periodic conditions introduce an additional challenge due to the Fourier modes interactions at high frequencies. This study overcomes this issue by analyzing the time evolution of the $H^s$-norm of the velocity field for any positive $s$. Unlike previous works, which relied on the Birkhoff theorem, this research uses time-averaging of the nonlinear Navier-Stokes equation in the BANM form, adapted from the Gevrey-type estimate. By considering all possible Fourier combinations, we show that the average rate of solution growth does not exceed $(1+\varepsilon)^{\frac{s}{6}}e^{2+\varepsilon}$ with excess exponent $\varepsilon$, where the constant $\varepsilon$ depends on the Fourier mode and its frequency. This result is validated for the case when the initial conditions belong to the $H^6$ space and we derive an upper limit on the Lyapunov exponents for the related linearized problem.

An essential requirement for quantum computing to advance is the ability to accurately perform and verify computations. The standard method for checking quantum calculations, which compares the outcomes with a predetermined model, fails to work properly when the input data is slightly incorrect due to the way it encodes information in quantum circuits. This leads to the creation of an efficient new approach for verifying quantum calculations that works by analyzing the circuit's structure and systematically verifying the calculations in a step-by-step manner from the starting point to the ending point. The process involves reorganizing the quantum circuit so that critical components are positioned near the starting point, which reduces the complexity of verification from exponential to linear complexity. The new method can successfully verify the calculations in scenarios where the input data is slightly incorrect, which is a common issue in quantum computing. This breakthrough makes it possible to reliably perform and verify computations in quantum computing.

Our query suggests that implicit neural networks may excel at creating realistic three-dimensional shapes for cells and could potentially generate novel cell forms. To demonstrate this, we employ an implicit neural volume representation, which enables the three-dimensional reconstruction of cells through a coordinate-based input, in this case, based on their morphology. By training a neural network implicitly, we find that it can learn a functional mapping that utilizes the input shape and underlying biological information to produce a realistic three-dimensional volume. Following successful training, we test the effectiveness of our approach by observing the generated cell forms, which not only resemble those of real, developing cells but also exhibit a high level of organ specificity. Furthermore, our method proves versatile, as we show that it can generate novel cell forms by adjusting either the shape or the underlying biological information. To the best of our knowledge, our implicit neural volume representation approach stands out from existing comparison methods focused on generating accurate and diverse cell forms.

Reinforcement learning techniques have successfully solved complex problems in artificial environments. Despite its effectiveness, its potential to influence our understanding of how organisms interact with their natural surroundings is considerable. The interaction between an organism and its environment can be seen as a dynamic process influenced by external stimuli, shaping its behavioral responses through reinforcement. By applying this learning theory to animal behavior, we aim to identify common environmental cues that contribute to the development of geographic knowledge, assuming it to be a learned skill rather than an inherent one. Our analysis, driven by a series of challenging reinforcement learning problems, has led us to devise a simple, flexible framework for modeling an organism's geographic awareness. According to this framework, an organism represents significant places with distinct features in an internal map, using memory to associate stimuli with these locations and learn their importance. The environmental cues that support learning new locations with memory are identified as places that can be easily recognized and visited again. Our findings suggest that these cues could have driven the development of geographic knowledge in organisms, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms that support exploration and learning in natural environments.

In the context of pilot-wave theories, we analyze the behavior of overdamped particles within a one-dimensional channel with a Harrow dimer, demonstrating that the particle's location forms a non-retrograde Markov chain. Building on this analysis, we explore the extension to multiple particles and introduce a new type of dipole, the hard-drive dimer, which serves as a practical implementation of the Harrow dimer. Additionally, we investigate the Scattering Hydrodynamic dimer and the Optical Tunnel dimer, both of which possess distinct differences from the hard-drive dimer.

The challenge of pinpointing the source of sound events within 3D space is tackled by a proposed method, which uses a convolutional recurrent neural network with rectangular filter length. To boost performance, a training technique involving channel rotation is applied to take full advantage of available data. Results show that this approach yields a source localization error of less than 2 degrees and sound event detection accuracy of around 0.9, both in terms of frame and SDR metrics.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems, like wireless orthogonal frequency division multiplexing, benefit from a system that mimics superposition in communication, making it possible to cater to users with varying data requirements while ensuring reliable data transfer to users with higher requirements. This concept is effectively represented through the Enchantment of Superposition principle, highlighting the trade-offs inherent in designing such systems for users with data requirements that may not always be the same. By understanding these trade-offs, network planners can make informed decisions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of superposition-based wireless systems, their performance metrics and optimization methods, focusing on systems with users that have the same data requirements, known as multi-user systems, and users with different data requirements, known as blind or opaque systems. It also explores a third category, known as channel state information (CSI)-aware systems, where users' data requirements are tied to the quality of the communication links. This paper examines various Opitmization problems in superposition-based wireless systems, focusing on efficient resource allocation, reliable data transfer, and optimal system performance. It also provides a detailed analysis of the current state of the art in superposition-based wireless systems, their potential applications, and future areas of research. This superposition-based wireless systems knowledge domain can benefit from research in relevant fields like wireless communication, optimization, and reinforcement learning.

The significance level of a signal's spectral domain analysis is directly tied to the number and shapes of its level contours. The assumptions underlying conventional spectral analysis methods, such as their lack of dependence on time and frequency, need to be reevaluated in light of new evidence suggesting their imperfect nature. As an alternative, we introduce a geometric approach that provides a more accurate analysis of signals through the study of their level contours' stochastic structure. This approach, referred to as SpectroGram, offers a deeper understanding of signals, enabling the development of more robust detection and estimation techniques. To verify its efficacy, SpectroGram is compared to conventional signal processing methods on simulated and real-world data. The results show that SpectroGram outperforms conventional methods in many cases.

We've developed a versatile technique for detecting traveling chimera patterns and synchronized groups in interconnected neural networks, regardless of their intrinsic properties. Using a measure derived from the dynamics of the network as a whole, we can identify areas where chaos meets order and extract various pattern types, from stable to dynamically complex states. This method refuses to compromise on the following: It doesn't make predictions about the network, rely on cumbersome calculations or rely on questionable assumptions. It only uses minimal, real-time readings of the system's state, applies a straightforward and lightweight analysis, and relies on straightforward visualization. Using this technique, we can distinguish traveling chimera patterns from stable patterns where different parts of the network behave differently. Furthermore, we can identify and monitor various types of patterns, from synchronized groups to dynamic patterns with multiple frequencies of oscillation. Our findings are accompanied by a free, open-source software tool, allowing easy reproduction and extension of our results for the community to use.

The random force method, initially created for 2-body systems, has been expanded and applied to n-body systems in a way that maintains efficiency. This method eliminates the need for precise orbital integration by modeling collisions as random events. A module implementing this method within the REBOUND code for post-Newtonian corrections is described, along with results from n-body simulations using this module.

Continuous feedback regulation, a crucial technique, allows designers to mold the behavior of open-loop chaotic systems through adjustment of a properly chosen measurable parameter, often referred to as a controller or regulator. This paper presents a comprehensive, quantum-inspired approach to modeling the feedback regulation of chaotic systems, employing the path-integral method and resulting in a formula applicable to a broad range of systems. We illustrate the utility of this approach by examining two complex systems: the first involves a class of systems governed by Lorenz-like dynamics, while the second focuses on the synchronization of two chaotic systems with tuning fork-like dynamics. In both cases, our approach enables the derivation of efficient quantum-inspired algorithms for calculating optimal feedback regulation paths.

For a channel filled with an incompressible fluid, an infinite number of solid spheres are added and the sequence of their arrival is alternated between placing them in the center and alternating sides of the channel. The resulting configuration is a two-dimensional packing where the spheres' positions are mirrored on either side of a central point. The steady-state packing density $\pi_0$ in this scenario is found to be 0.3468, which is nearly 10% higher than the densest packing density for spheres in three-dimensional space, and significantly higher than the density of an ordinary liquid.

Research into El Ni\~no events has concentrated on examining the impacts of different forms on global climate patterns, yet the focus has mainly been on S-ENSO (El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation). A recent analysis aims to contribute to a broader understanding by investigating the distinct seasonal precipitation patterns in various ENSO types across different altitude ranges. Using temperature-derived precipitation data, the study analyzes the spatial extent of precipitation across different elevations during 1979-2019, revealing distinct responses to both core and non-core ENSO phenomena. Core phenomena, comprising eastern Pacific warming and chlorophyll depletion in the equatorial Pacific, were found to produce uniform precipitation effects. In contrast, non-core events exhibited more complex behavior, influencing precipitation in the equatorial and Pacific regions outside of the standard observation area. Notably, the study discovers that non-core events exhibit more pronounced and region-specific precipitation responses compared to core phenomena, particularly around mountainous regions in the equatorial Pacific and the African great lakes. These findings imply the need for non-core ENSO consideration in understanding regional precipitation variations during extreme events.

We suggest that galaxies like Leo I, which have extremely low star formation rates, 
can provide valuable information about the processes involved in the development of massive black holes at their cores. It is assumed that high mass flows through the core region are the result of a massive black hole consuming matter. We propose that galaxies like Leo I, characterized by their weak central star formation, may represent the final stages of a proposed model for black hole development, in which matter flows are initially directed at smaller, less central black holes within a network of smaller, unresolved clusters. Over time, these smaller black holes merge to form a central massive black hole, and the surrounding reservoir of gravitationally bound matter, which may include a substantial amount of the core's mass, is then directed at the new, more centralized massive black hole. This process could explain the observed relationship between a galaxy's central mass flow rate and its mass, particularly the lack of a lower bound to this relationship. Additionally, this scenario could potentially account for an observed, irregular pattern in the core masses of galaxies. Further study of galaxies like Leo I, along with observations of their central star formation, core mass flows, and large scale metal distribution, could provide valuable insight into the processes involved in the development of massive black holes at their cores.

In systems with electronic flat bands, unusual correlation effects can arise due to strong interactions between electrons.  Frustrated magnetism and superconductivity can emerge in such systems, making them particularly intriguing.  Recent discoveries have led to the identification of flat band induced magnetism in certain materials, although a corresponding effect on their electronic transport has yet to be closely examined.

This study focuses on the transport properties of Co-doped SnSe, a mineral with a Kagome structure that exhibits a flat band at its Fermi level.  Coinciding with a medium-range ordering of Co ions within the lattice, the material exhibits two distinct resistivity peaks at temperatures of 105 and 175 K.  The existence of multiple orbits and electron interactions within the system suggests that spin-orbit coupling and long-range Co ordering synergistically contribute to the resistivity peaks, distinguishing them from typical magnetism-induced effects.  The observed resistivity peaks disappear when the material's magnetic order disappears, indicating that they are directly related to flat band induced magnetism within the system.  This study provides a unique example of how correlations within a flat band can significantly impact a material's transport properties.

The unravelling of the human genome has brought us to the threshold of understanding the intricate mechanisms governing the most basic and essential aspects of our existence. Despite significant breakthroughs, the complex relationships between our genetic constitution and traits like height, weight and intelligence remain shrouded in uncertainty. To shed light on these phenomena, we've brought together experts from various fields of study to share their data and findings on 18 key characteristics, encompassing physical qualities, health conditions and cognitive abilities. This dataset provides a wealth of new insights and questions, and by making it publicly available, we hope to stimulate research and foster a novel approach to understanding the multifaceted nature of human biology.

We establish and present a comprehensive list of all block arrangements, denoted as $(r,\lambda)$, that have a unique greatest common divisor with $r$, along with their corresponding linear groups that provide flag-transitive symmetry to arrange these blocks within an $r$-dimensional space. Additionally, we identify the cases where the symmetry groups exert their transitive action on the flags, which are components of the arrangeement.

To study the individual characteristics of particles in confined atomic systems, 
we (i) calculate stationary states of an atom-like three-body system with Coulomb
interaction confined within a harmonic potential, 
then (ii) evaluate distribution functions for particle locations, 
and finally (iii) calculate information entropies of particles with and without considering
interparticle interactions. 
Our analysis shows that when the harmonic potential surpasses the atomic interaction,
marked by a confining potential energy equal to the 8th Rydberg energy of the relative motion,
the spatial pattern of one particle influences the others. 
The information entropies of the system, whether considering interaction or not, 
exhibits similarities with those of Bose particles confined in an harmonic potential. 
However, this resemblance holds under specific conditions regarding the particle number and
temperature. 
If the temperature is higher than the equivalent zener temperature, 
the system, whether interacting or not, becomes indistinguishable from a system of free Bose particles.

The Large Extensive Binary System in Andromeda, also known as M31, has been studied by multiple studies in the past to verify the predictions made by the Newtonian gravity model and to observe the effects of gravitational phenomenon on the binary system. A recent study conducted an extensive examination of LEBS in M31 to determine the extent to which its components conform to the extensive binary model. This analysis revealed that two out of three binary systems in M31 that were studied, adhere to the extensive binary model, and the results of the third binary were inconclusive due to a lack of data. The study also compared its results with the predictions made by the extensive binary model, and the outcomes were similar to what was previously reported, indicating that the extensive binary model is compatible with the observed properties of the binary systems in M31.

In multiplicative linear logic with multiplex and co-multiplex, a novel sequence of sequent calculations is formulated to replace cut-elimination, which we term 'cut-elimination through decomposition'. This method achieves the same level of computational efficiency as standard cut-elimination procedures. We also introduce a revised framework that incorporates cut-elimination through decomposition, making it applicable in multiplicative linear logic with multiplex and co-multiplex, while maintaining equivalence to cut-elimination procedures.

In finance, as in other fields, predicting the health of correlated time series is a crucial issue, yet it's extremely challenging. Determining the likelihood of stable correlation in advance can facilitate high-risk, time-sensitive investment decisions. This study develops a predictive framework to assess the fate of correlated financial time series, leveraging cross-recurrence diagrams and their scalar embeddings to forecast their synchronization condition. To establish predictive models, the study employs machine learning algorithms, specifically support vector machines and random forests, using nonlinear, non-stationary financial time series from major global markets. The results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting stable correlations, with our best model achieving a remarkable 85% accuracy in forecasting the fate of synchronized time series.

THz radiation induces a driving force similar to optical radiation, thereby triggering electronic excitation and vibrational motion within a material. By leveraging its tunable frequency and amplitude, researchers can examine the material's response electronics, as well as its interaction with electrons and vibrations. The application of THz radiation can reveal new physics, such as electron pairing, superconductivity, and magnetic ordering, and can potentially control magnetic properties by aligning spins. Additionally, researchers can utilize its immense influence to study highly resistant or highly anisotropic materials. The experiments described in this study investigates the electronic and vibrational interactions within a 2D graphene monolayer and ferromagnetic graphene bilayer, demonstrating electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions driven by THz radiation. The research reveals new physics, such as the graphite monolayer exhibiting mode-selective coupling and mode-dose gating, whereas the magnetic graphene bilayer shows promise for controlling spin orders via vibrational motion. The study on the magnetic graphene bilayer offers a means to manipulate magnetic properties at the nanoscale, offering a fresh pathway in graphene research and potential technological applications.

Current commercial systems predicting click-through-rates (CTR) often disregard the content of new ads when making predictions, as their visual elements can't be extracted easily like natural language. To address this, our research proposes an enhanced CTR forecasting model that incorporates information from ad images. At the heart of our approach lies an image feature extractor, which uses co-occurrence patterns in past ads to determine similar images. This allows our model to obtain visual features for each user and correlate them with historical ads using collaborative filtering, resulting in a predictive model of user reactions to ad visual content. Our results show that this approach surpasses traditional CTR forecasting models by an average of 3.16% (relative 0.91%) in validating data and 2.64% (relative 0.84%) in real-world trials.

Improving object-oriented software design through constraint analysis has proven benefits, yet business process modeling and compliance checking tools frequently overlook the constraints that truly define a business's operational landscape.  This paper highlights the significance of constraints in business process engineering and proposes an approach to retroactively apply constraints to existing process models, thus aligning them with the principles of Design by Contract.  This technique is demonstrated using an example drawn from the BPMN 2.0 standard, illustrated through a UML-based case tool model, and the associated tool documentation will outline the technical details of this constraint analysis method.

Wildfires affecting the atmospheric system have far-reaching consequences on the planet's energy balance, food security, and human well-being. However, precise forecasting of wildfires remains challenging due to the non-linearity, non-stationarity, and spatiotemporal complexity of fire aerosols. To address this issue, researchers have turned to advanced data-driven approaches, inclusive of machine learning and deep learning techniques, for improved forecasting. This study develops a novel physics-informed statistical framework that leverages the collective information from multiple geostationary satellite datasets to create a single, coherent product. By integrating the dynamics of wildfire aerosols and utilizing hierarchical deep learning architecture, the researchers have successfully demonstrated the ability to generate smoke maps, simulate fire spread, and predict fire intensity. Notably, the proposed framework has outperformed existing methods in forecasting wildfire aerosols, yielding superior results and thereby contributing to environmental modeling and climate modeling. The associated code is publicly accessible on GitHub at the provided URL.

This research investigates the balance between maintaining user anonymity and accurately pinpointing their location in a tracked area. We have developed an algorithm that estimates a user's actual location within a certain location region, taking into consideration any relevant previous data. Our method is comparable to, yet more efficient than, the current approach. We have demonstrated that through the use of statistical relationships between locations, the extent of location uncertainty can be reduced. Additionally, we have created a simulation environment to verify the effectiveness of our algorithm in various scenarios.

Accurate estimation of brain connectivity from multisite resting-state fMRI data is crucial for unbiased brain function research and will be even more vital with the upcoming large-scale human connectome project. We developed a novel approach to estimate connectivity that correctly accounts for data from multiple sources, featuring degrees of freedom assigned to estimate parameters, tight constraints imposed on estimated connections, and efficient assignment of degrees of freedom with minimal information loss. This approach allows us to compare the accuracy of other methods, such as fixed and free approaches, by varying the degrees of freedom without re-estimating parameters. Results show that reducing degrees of freedom dramatically decreases prediction error in a wide range of scenarios, and even mild restrictions dramatically decrease error when the restriction's effect size is small and indirectly affects the edges. We also found that restricting edge values below a certain threshold can improve the accuracy of edge estimation while maintaining overall connectivity estimates.

The study of directed network's Ricci curvature has been emerging, in contrast to the theory of undirected networks which has established far-reaching applications in many fields. This research presents a new approach by introducing a lower bound for the Ricci curvature on directed networks, resulting in a stronger concentration of measure phenomenon compared to undirected networks. Specifically, under this curvature constraint, it is demonstrated that the concentration of measure phenomenon occurs within a minimally small radius, independent of the directed network's Euler-Lagrange equation eigenvalues. Furthermore, a growth rate of the spectral gap is obtained as a function of the radius, and a comparison with the efficient convergence rate in simple directed networks is also provided. Additionally, it is shown that any directed network satisfying the curvature constraint can be embedded in a new directed network with efficient convergence rate, which has applications in many fields.

Language models that support code-mixing have gained significant interest recently, given the prevalence of language mixing in various cultures, especially in urban areas. Code-mixing is a form of multilingual speech or writing that combines two or more officially recognized languages. It often occurs in urban settings where individuals speak two or more languages in everyday life. This research focuses on code-mixing, and our experiments use a Romanian-English language model, known as RoEn, as our test case. We aimed to enhance our results by introducing a new dynamic encoding method, and by making positional encoding relative within a sentence. Positional encoding is typically used when word order varies significantly from expected norms. There are two primary issues with traditional positional encoding: it often conveys redundant information and can easily become overfit, especially when word order is inconsistent. We present a new positional encoding method, PESTO, that is relative, not absolute. It depends on nearby words within a sentence, as opposed to a fixed sequence. This innovative approach has several benefits. Firstly, it reduces redundant information. Secondly, it minimizes overfitting by limiting the encoding to nearby words. Our experiments indicate that PESTO outperforms existing models, and we also introduce a new transition point encoding method to further improve results.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure and temperature. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly affects the variation of the critical temperature with pressure. Additionally, we found that considering the variable density of states does not alter its isotope-induced shift. Our research also demonstrates that assuming a constant density of states overestimates the influence of isotope substitution on the electronic self-energy and related superconducting properties. Therefore, using a constant density of states may not provide an accurate quantitative prediction of the superconducting properties of 3H-S and potentially other hydride superconductors.

Fisher made several key statements about the direction of gene action within the context of the Hardy-Wincoln model. We contend that the fundamental principle underlying his conclusions has been overlooked. By re-examining the relationships between gene action, inheritance ratios, and covariances, we provide a straightforward explanation for Fisher's findings. Our analysis confirms that Fisher's mean effect accurately represents the combined action of multiple genes contributing to a single trait. Furthermore, we believe a clear understanding of Fisher's mean effect effectively communicates the collective direction of gene action, while an alternative measure incorporating interaction terms fails to serve this purpose. Fisher's mean effect is demonstrated to conform to the principle of homogeneity of direction, although it does not conform to the principle of additivity. We illustrate the causal significance of Fisher's mean effect by using an analogy of gears in a machine, where the mean effect is comparable to the overall direction of gear action before considerations of interactions or reversals are taken into account.

This paper presents a novel and efficient approach to improve the stability of a bipedal robot through propellant-assisted locomotion. By integrating propulsion and ambulation, this method optimizes energy usage for longer mission durations. Two key parameters for efficient bipedal movement, namely the step period and propulsion strength, are identified through a dynamic analysis of this ambulation-assisted gait. This study demonstrates that the relationship between these parameters and specific system characteristics can be generalized. This generalized relationship provides designers with a valuable tool for evaluating the feasibility of ambulation-assisted gait and optimizing system performance for longer durations.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel maps to streamline the process. By leveraging a pre-built surfel map, we eliminate the need for a comprehensive point cloud dataset or pose library, thereby facilitating easier and more cost-effective environment preparations. Upon instance selection, our method extracts structural features from 2D images and conducts a surfel-based pose search, utilizing both feature matching and 3D geometry constraints to optimize the solution. Both our offline and online surfel building approaches contribute to accurate relocalization performance, with the option to tailor the surfel map to the specific requirements of the target localization task. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art baseline techniques on a KITTI dataset, with the added capability to function without any prior knowledge of the environment.

Label-driven knowledge sharing between multiple parties is hindered by several issues in current approaches. Firstly, model updates from the server may not accurately reflect the preferences of individual clients, as the aggregation process lacks sufficient clarity. Secondly, proposed solutions relying on statistical assumptions about client data distributions are often insufficient for real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel technique called CRFSS, which allows for decentralized semi-supervised learning with optimized model updates and tailored loss functions. By reducing uncertainty about both data and labels, CRFSS enhances the relevance of model updates and improves overall performance.

The collision of a black hole and a neutron star produces a dynamic and dynamic system influenced by the interaction of general relativity, magnetohydrodynamics, and radiative transfer. In the context of simulations employing approximate general relativity and magnetohydrodynamics with a simplified model of neutrino emission, the resulting merger process is thoroughly explored. By simulating the merger under diverse initial and computational configurations, a comprehensive understanding of the resulting merger is achieved. The outcomes of these simulations, obtained with approximately 1.5 million grid zones, are compared and contrasted. The simulation results in a massive accretion disk, forming a massive disk with a central black hole and an expansive disk without magnetic field polarization. A distorted metric of a given Riemann surface means a specific deviation from its original complex structure. Researchers have discovered that for any Riemann surface, there exists a unique distorted metric with a specific characteristic - its first Chern class remains unchanged. This distortion metric, first introduced by Tyomel'kin in 1983, has since been extensively studied by many mathematicians. In a recent paper, the first Chern class of a specific family of distortion metrics on arbitrary closed Riemann surfaces has been investigated. It has been shown that the second cohomology class of these surfaces is necessary for expressing the first Chern class of their distortion metrics, as proven by Tyomel'kin, but also sufficient in certain situations. This provides a comprehensive answer to a previously posed question by Tyomel'kin.

This note builds on the work of Herer and Robbins starting in 1997, and provides a straightforward proof that shows a sequence of approximating Q-processes can converge uniformly to the true Q-process under minimal conditions. The only requirements are that the Q-processes must be ergodic Markov chains, sharing the same state space with the true Q-process, and possessing a common stationary distribution. Additionally, the sequence must be such that the difference in their transition probabilities is consistent across all states.

The mechanism of THz surface plasmon-induced adhesion of nanoparticles to a graphene surface is investigated in detail. It has been demonstrated that two unique features emerge in the graphene's electrostatic response when its doping level is in the range of $10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$. These distinct characteristics lead to the generation of two directed electric fields that trap at the surface of the graphene, creating an environment in which nanoparticles can become firmly attached to the graphene surface through a combination of van der Waals forces and electrostatic attraction. A study conducted using a combined finite-difference time-domain and hypergeometric approach provides in-depth insights into the electromagnetic interactions between the graphene surface, the nanoparticles, and the intervening medium. Our analysis reveals that nanoparticles can be drawn towards the graphene surface with an acceleration of $10^3$ cm/s^2 and are eventually fixed in place with an attachment force that exceeds the maximum force range of typical optical tweezers by over three orders of magnitude. This finding may be useful for implementing an ultra-potent optical trap capable of capturing thousands to millions of particles per second, which could lead to groundbreaking breakthroughs in the fields of nanotechnology, materials science and biotechnology.

In the optimal timing of medical interventions, the typical course of treatment often overrides rare patient outcomes, resulting in "too soon, too late, or too much" scenarios. To address this, a study is conducted to establish standard response curves for the duration of medical interventions, using data from an emergency department. With over 230,000 patient records and 20 different types of medical care, the study relies on complex modeling and simulation to determine how treatment time affects outcomes, while also accounting for varying patient health and provider treatment strategies. The results from both methods are compared to establish reliable intervention windows for commonly treated conditions, such as peptic ulcer bleeding and fracture management, providing guidelines for future studies and clinical decisions.

Our research focuses on how robots working together can accomplish a shared goal, particularly in situations where individual robots have limited local information and are only aware of their immediate surroundings. Each robot can only communicate with a small number of neighboring robots and has a local view restricted to these neighbors. To address this challenge, we have developed a new theoretical framework that enables a single central agent to coordinate with multiple robots and devise a collaborative strategy. The central agent can plan for the other robots by simulating their local views, allowing them to participate in the decision-making process. The theoretical framework provides a precise estimate of the differences between the central agent's choices and the optimal actions that would be taken through collective decision-making. To verify the theoretical framework, we have performed a series of experiments using simulations that aim to answer two crucial questions: (1) how accurately can the central agent replicate the outcomes of collective decision-making processes, and (2) what are the benefits and limitations of the central agent's ability to plan for the other robots. The results show that the central agent's predictions become increasingly accurate as the duration of the collaboration extends over many time steps. The efficiency gains from central planning are also dependent on specific circumstances: when the underlying network structure allows robots to effectively communicate with each other over extended periods, central planning can lead to superior outcomes; however, in networks that are poorly connected, central planning may not provide significant advantages.

The status of the Chiral Magnetic Effect's influence on the experimental data is assessed by analyzing the correlation between charges in collisions of lead ions at two different energy levels. The effect is minimized when measuring the specific combination of charge dependencies, and any remaining influence is likely negligible. This outcome contributes to constraining theoretical models involving specific spin-orbit coupling phenomena and provides foundational insight into the effective mass and magnitude of the chiral magnetic effect.

The surge in online crowdfunding has prompted a plethora of research into the factors that influence successful fundraising campaigns. To expand upon existing knowledge and avoid platform-specific biases, this study employs a combined quantitative and qualitative approach to investigate and compare the characteristics of successful campaigns on three platforms: GitHub, Indiegogo, and Kickstarter. The analysis focuses on crowd behaviors associated with campaign success, bearing in mind that context-dependent variables can influence crowdfunding dynamics. The findings uncover distinct crowd behaviors in each platform, with GitHub exhibiting a rapid and diverse feedback process, Indiegego exhibiting a gradual and less frequent feedback process, and Kickstarter in the middle. Synergy between funders and fundees is a common denominator for success across all three platforms. It is concluded that a rich feedback process is crucial for gaining momentum, whereas a balanced relationship between funders and fundees is key to long-term success.

As cyber threats evolve, organizations struggle to defend against them, partly due to the limited availability of certain types of cyber data sets. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach to address this issue by enabling collaborative cyber hazard research without revealing the details of individual organizations. It achieves this through a novel framework that allows multiple sources to contribute to the training of a unified model for network intrusion detection, without the need to gather data from a single source. The framework's effectiveness was tested using 15 data sets from real-world incidents in various industries, and the results showed that the collaborative training lasted for 51 iterations before performance discrepancies arose between the central node and local nodes. This innovative approach was validated by comparing its results to those gained from a traditional approach using combined data sets, and experiments confirmed its benefits.

A robotic system's ability to perform a task efficiently in a minimal amount of time is heavily dependent on the sequence in which it carries out the required actions. This time optimization is particularly important in the processing of visual information and can be achieved through a time-consuming process of sequence generation. A more efficient approach is desired to meet real-time requirements. The majority of existing methods either generate a limited number of high-quality sequences or quickly generate a large number of poor-quality sequences. In this research, a novel method is presented that rapidly generates an optimal sequence of actions for a stable and rigid object's manipulation by a multi-point robotic system. The sequence is optimized to reduce the object's deformation and minimize the distance between the robotic hands' grasp points. The method employs a sequence-based solution similar to the K-means clustering method, but with an adjusted clustering process that produces high-quality sequences. The method's effectiveness is validated through simulations that compare its performance to existing methods.

This research addresses the underpinnings of ultra-high speed and flexible SiMOSFETs.
A key challenge in achieving high performance lies in the device's electrical
properties, whereas manufacturing complexities pose a relatively smaller
obstacle. Therefore, integrating a conventional 300mm CMOS process with
silicided gates to produce MOSFETs with high mobility marks an important step
towards overcoming manufacturing hurdles. By examining the structural
parameters of the gate, channel, and drain, we can accurately control the
device's threshold voltage, further enabling the design of customizable
devices. In this context, we present a set of highly agile SiMOSFETs with
variable number of gates, along with a comprehensive 1D mathematical model
that accurately replicates the mobility and the DC output characteristics of
these devices. Moreover, our model demonstrates a strong correlation with
3D numerical device simulations.

In the context of coupled oscillators, systems with diverse frequencies or properties are typically expected to remain asynchronous, with a stable equilibrium state. However, our research reveals that, under appropriate conditions, a group of oscillators with different characteristics can achieve a shared rhythmic movement, including a wide array of movement patterns. We demonstrate that these conditions rely heavily on the individual oscillator models used, as well as the specific connections between oscillators, with inner relationships potentially playing a crucial role in determining whether a shared rhythm is achieved. Our findings have significant implications for the study of team dynamics in sociology and management, suggesting that diverse teams can achieve synchronized movement through various mechanisms.

A significant issue in automated systems, including search algorithms, is bias, particularly in the outcomes they produce which can result in underrepresented groups being excluded from opportunities. This paper focuses on detecting and evaluating a particular type of bias, namely Origin Variety Bias, which occurs when algorithmic systems favor individuals who share the same background or characteristics as the inquiry origin. We propose using computer-generated characters called virtual agents to simulate different origins and monitor search outcomes, which allows for the quantification of Origin Variety Bias. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through experiments conducted on YouTube, where we identify a bias that favors videos uploaded by users with similar cultural backgrounds to the search query.

A technique called "amplitude matching" is used to accurately determine monodromy deformations of the Wess-Zumino model at three loops. This method leverages the fact that these deformations have a straightforward, one-to-one correlation with relevant coupling constants in the underlying scalar field theory. By comparing monodromy deformations in the Wess-Zumino model with predictions from a conventional scalar field perspective, researchers claim to identify novel, non-trivial loop effects that weren't apparent at two-loop levels. To achieve this, researchers analyzed four-loop amplitudes in N=1*Wess-Zumino model, specifically considering planar configurations with two distinct legs. Notably, this study successfully bridges the gap between theoretical understanding of gauge theories and string theory, specifically through its connection to the shear transformation in N=1*U(1) shear connection of string theory.
We prove that there is exactly one elliptic curve, up to uniqueness, defined over a cubic Galois field that has a point on the curve as its reduction and a 13-rank point at infinity.

In complex wireless systems, interference correlation poses significant challenges to system performance, largely because existing medium access control protocols assume independent interference with limited success. We introduce a new adaptive medium access control approach that addresses interference correlation via a probabilistic channel-aware access strategy, yielding notable performance gains in terms of increased throughput and link reliability under demanding system efficiency metrics. Its correlation-aware counterpart, leveraging channel estimation, achieves even better results although it incurs higher feedback and processing costs, namely an exponential increase in this context.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in pseudo-labeling, many previously used methods have been unable to reliably produce reliable pseudo-labels, particularly in graph classification tasks where a significant proportion of nodes can pose an labeling risk. One major problem is the GNN's weak ability to generalize to nodes that are far away from the labeled nodes. Another issue lies in the fact that gradient-based methods are often unable to produce meaningful pseudo-labels for graph-level tasks. In order to address these limitations, we propose Local Pseudo-Label, a novel pseudo-labeling method for graph nodes that utilizes a two-phase training process. In the first phase, the model is trained to accumulate representation entropy at labeled nodes, allowing it to effectively integrate information from all labeled nodes. In the second phase, the model generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled nodes by leveraging the influence of the labeled nodes. In order to prevent the propagation of errors in the local phase, we have also developed a novel regularization technique called Confusing Supervised. Experimental results on widely-used benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over current techniques.

In video processing tasks, precise movement detection between frames is crucial, but it can be computationally expensive. This research introduces PatchNet, a convolutional neural network that efficiently captures connections between frames by tracking patches instead of entire images. By doing so, it reduces the complexity of frame-to-frame movements, enabling easier training. Since only nearby patches are relocated, not the entire image, less information needs to be shifted during the training process, making it feasible to achieve good results using a smaller model. Due to its depth-wise convolutions and the localization of movement, PatchNet uses significantly fewer parameters compared to typical neural networks. This architecture enables successful application to previous methods for video segmentation, video interpolation, and video super-resolution, often with notable improvements.

We examine a system of one-dimensional highway traffic modeled by a TASEE, a version of the TASEP system with a limited number of periodic sections, to determine how drivers distribute themselves within the highway. Given a traffic system with a specific flow capacity and multiple distinct periodic segments of varying lengths, we develop a method to distribute drivers in such a way that maximizes their overall travel times. Our approach involves calculating a vector that represents the desired distribution of drivers in each period of the highway's cycles, based on a system of equations that account for traffic flow and a specific origin in the highway. Notably, we are able to provide an exact solution for a specific case involving a single periodic segment of traffic. Our results are relevant to understanding how drivers allocate themselves in a system of periodic highway traffic.

A future generation of wireless communication systems is envisioned that integrates data and power transmission capabilities. The combined approach, known as SWIPT, enables efficient use of available energy in wireless networks by eliminating the need for expensive and bulky power sources. To optimize SWIPT performance, a novel resource allocation technique is proposed, which maximizes the throughput of each service while ensuring sufficient power for all users. This is achieved through two distinct methods: a convex optimization solution and a corresponding heuristic strategy, providing accurate and efficient solutions, respectively. Simulation results demonstrate that both methods significantly boost the throughput of SWIPT systems compared to conventional time-division between data and power transmission techniques. Furthermore, the proposed heuristic strategy efficiently balances power allocation and data transmission rates, closely matching the performance of the complex optimization solution.

We show that Pauli's exclusion principle has a broader impact in Fermi fluids composed of fermions with a repulsive interaction than previously thought, affecting both superfluid properties and instantaneous behavior in general PA fermion systems, revealing a new principle in Fermi physics beyond Pauli's principle.

We present a simple electrical circuit that effectively models conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, accurately capturing its key characteristics and dynamics. The proposed circuit is readily buildable using commonly available components and, through coherent displacement driving, generates Sauter-type nonlinear resonant forces similar to those found in optical systems. By adjusting the mechanical impedance, it is possible to achieve a converted power that approaches the maximum available from an ideal amplifier. Furthermore, this circuit offers a means to study classical nonlinearity in mechanical systems and presents potential applications in the development of advanced electrical filters and processors for mechanical signals.

This research paper examines a broad category of polynomials originating from the Airy function's expansion, referencing their co-associative, commutative, and unital properties which stem from their connection to a sub-2-category involving 3-morphisms. The paper identifies and proves a universal identity for these polynomials, solving related differential equations and establishing a relationship with the extended symmetries of the Airy function in the process. Additionally, the paper discusses a theoretical framework for the polynomials, providing a recursive construction method and a natural isomorphism to the symmetric series of a graph associated with a finite poset that has ascension-based order.

This study investigates the behavior of robots moving in a straight line in a dense robotic assembly when the robots are unable to maintain a constant speed. Building on a model initially exploring unpredictable movements, the research examines how uneven robot movements affect the robots' behavior, specifically their gap size, and reveals that altering a single factor can reverse the robots' local behavior, resulting in some robots accelerating and others slowing down. To better understand this phenomenon, the researchers introduced and mathematically derived a new order parameter to describe and analyze the local behavior of the robotic assembly. Additionally, the research validates the findings through simulations of robots moving according to a toy model, and the authors speculate on the implications of these discoveries for future robotic assembly applications.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Preoperative patient preparation is crucial for a successful laparoscopic surgery. One essential step involves assessing the patient's stomach for food residue using a fibruscope to determine if the surgery can proceed safely. This process is prolonged if the stomach contains food, which hinders the visualization of the desired images for the doctor to make a decision. Researchers often employ image processing techniques to extract valuable insights from these images to make decision-making easier. To date, most approaches focus on extracting useful information from raw images, which are often distorted and difficult to interpret. To address this, this study suggests using smoke detection as a smoke-free preparation advantage (SFA) metric, which measures the reduction in processing time required to prepare for surgery. To achieve this, the proposed method combines noise filtering and smoke detection using a deep neural network to provide a smoke-free preparation advantage score. Noise removal enhances the image quality, which in turn facilitates smoke detection, allowing for faster preparation times. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which outperforms existing smoke detection methods and provides a meaningful measure of the smoke-free preparation advantage.

This research introduces a technique for creating stable molecular gates on a specific type of ion trap, where multiple vibrational modes work together to facilitate gate operations. Using both analytical and simulation methods, we examine how different gate performance metrics are influenced by various trap settings and parameters. We find a specific set of conditions that allows for the creation of long-lived molecular ions with nearly identical frequencies and excellent coherence, which is essential for generating durable entanglement between these molecules.

Using temperature-dependent atomic pair distribution function analysis and molecular dynamics simulations, our research reveals the detailed atomic structures of the paraelectric phases in specific bismuth and gold-doped ferroelectric samples. By creating a temporary template with dynamic constraints mimicking the collective behavior of ions during polarization, our results offer a theoretical explanation for the unusual phenomena observed in the paraelectric phases of these materials. Our study provides a necessary step towards a more in-depth understanding of the microstructures present in the paraelectric phases of these materials, which are essential for developing the next generation of superconducting and quantum electronic devices.

Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for the relationship between specific components of the multivariate data. The resulting models include the multivariate Gaussian distribution with a sparsity-pattern specified by a graph, known as the Gaussian graphical model. This type of model can be extended to process data by representing the interdependence between components with a covariance matrix that has embedded zeros, based on a graph whose edges indicate non-zero dependencies. The resulting framework is known as the functional Gaussian graphical framework. A specific instance of this framework is the functional Gaussian graphical model, where the functional nature of the data is accounted for by using a kernel or operator on one of the variables. The application of this framework to process data is shown to be a more general case, known as the Gaussian process graphical model. This model allows for the interdependence between components of multivariate Gaussian processes that change over space or time, based on a sparsity-pattern specified by a graph, with each node of the graph representing a location or time point. Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for the relationship between specific components of the multivariate data.
