experimental $\alpha$ cross-section data, and a reliable $\sigma_\alpha$ 
is derived for $^{51}$V+$^{6}$Li reaction, which meets the criteria for 
$^{62}$V establishment.

A previously (2019) presented study at the IEEE ICRA had highlighted the effectiveness of using tendon-based robotics to achieve versatile and flexible actuation capabilities. These capabilities facilitate a seamless transition between extension and retraction motions, unlike traditional joint-based robots that usually experience increased resistance during the reverse process. Building upon this foundation, this updated study revisits the design of robotic systems with tendon-based execution and expands the scope by exploring their application in climbing mechanisms. These mechanisms are inspired by the anatomy of certain eels which, interestingly, exhibit preferential movement in specific directions despite having muscle groups that provide bi-directional movement. This research demonstrates the creation of a robotic system with tendon-based actuation and showcases its implementation in an innovative, general-purpose climbing mechanism. Experimental results are presented to validate the improved performance of this novel mechanism.

We present a probabilistic model of colon cancer immunotherapy reaction based on the Fokker-Planck equation, which simulates the dynamics of the immune system's response to treatment. The Fokker-Planck equation is solved through two distinct numerical methods: a finite difference approach and a Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation. Building upon this model, we developed an optimization technique to identify the most effective treatment strategy for maximum immune system response. The proposed model and optimization method offer a valuable tool for clinical decision-making in colon cancer immunotherapy, allowing healthcare professionals to select the most suitable treatment variant to achieve optimal patient outcomes.

The increasing demand for faster data transfer is driving the development of new techniques, with Wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication emerging as a leading method to improve network efficiency and speed. In this study, we develop an scheduling approach based on real-time data analysis. The method uses deep learning to optimize the transmission process, allowing a greater number of devices to transmit data at the same time while minimizing interference. The approach consists of two phases: a real-time database and a deep learning algorithm. The database records the characteristics of each device's transmission environment, while the deep learning algorithm predicts optimal scheduling options using this information. The effectiveness of this method was tested in simulations under varying network conditions, with results showing significant improvements over traditional scheduling techniques. The method achieved an enhanced data transfer rate and a lower error rate for longer messages. The best results were seen with a certain level of network congestion. The approach offers a rapid response to changing network conditions, with the ability to adapt to different network configurations. The algorithm's efficiency may be influenced by the specific technology used in the network.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [27] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic flow. This current work examines helicity in a more complex scenario - compressible flow with no viscosity and barotropic density. To do this, we define "conservation law density" and "helicity density", deriving their vector fields from specific properties of the fluid's internal energy. By establishing that these densities along with their corresponding gradient lie on the same parallel in a specific Lie algebra, we prove the non-conservation of helicity in the case of smooth solutions to the compressible Euler equations, assuming that the fluid does not contain any rotational motion. On the other hand, we prove the conservation of helicity in the case of the fluid being strictly hyperbolic critical points without any rotation.

The researchers in a particular study demonstrated that in an explicitly defined two-component Bose-Einstein condensate model, a specific type of instability occurs when linearly propagating interfaces are presented. Furthermore, it was found that a significant increase in reflection occurs at certain limits of wave number. By applying a new approach, it was possible to explain this phenomenon. Utilizing this approach, it was determined that a significant maximum in reflection exists at a specific limit of wave number. Using numerical simulations, it was confirmed that this maximum occurs in regions where a particular type of instability is present in the system.

The likelihood of detecting a second gravitational wave from a compact binary inspiral by LIGO or VIRGO should be increased if they target orbits that have remaining eccentricities greater than $10^{-3}. We have computed new predictions for the average remaining eccentricities of inspiraling binaries using advanced gravitational wave theories, which will help improve the efficiency of detection criteria. It is also proposed that binaries with eccentricities between $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-3}$ be designated as 'partially inspiral' events, a new category that could bridge the gap between binary black hole identification and other areas of gravitational physics, such as binary neutron star mergers.

A proposed hybrid amplifier, combining a laser and a parametric converter, has the potential to significantly boost the output of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators, which are currently limited by their gain. This hybrid system could produce high-intensity, coherent X-ray pulses with elevated repetition rates, making it suitable for applications such as nonlinear spectroscopy, absorption microscopy, and coherent imaging. Notably, the hybrid amplifier's performance comes close to the maximum gain that a FEO can achieve, which is the gain that the oscillation itself provides. This hybrid system has the potential to be developed into a high-repetition-rate, high-intensity X-ray source that is already demonstrated in a FEO and can be used to explore various applications. This proposal is based on the simulation results of the hybrid's energy growth, spectral expansion, and pulse duration, which indicate that it can overcome the low saturation level limitation of a FEO and increase its useful applications.

Identifying unusual behavior in dynamic networks is crucial for uncovering plotless crimes and reducing social disorder. The challenge lies in recognizing incidents from time-varying network structures and node attribute patterns. Existing methods are limited to static networks or use the same weighted edges for all time points, ignoring incident-specific relationships. This paper addresses a novel problem by learning incident patterns from dynamic networks with evolving connections. The result is a method for detecting incidents based on node attribute patterns and the shift in network connections at specific time points. The method outperforms competing approaches on synthetic and real-world data, including an online dataset of disorder incidents in New York City. The experiment demonstrates that incident patterns are largely consistent but occasionally modified to adapt with changing network dynamics.

The nature of a collapsing shock wave in a variable density medium remains unclear, particularly as it approaches a specific density ratio. Numerical simulations conducted using two distinct methods: a Generalized Navier-Stokes equation incorporating fluid fluctuations, and a self-consistent fluid approach assuming fluctuations originate from turbulent motion, yield contrasting results. While the fluctuation-based method suggests shock collapse occurs in a variable density medium, the fluctuation-ignoring approach predicts it does not. This discrepancy highlights a long-standing unresolved problem in both astrophysics and fluid dynamics. Our study demonstrates that turbulent motion can be effectively modeled as a probabilistic density distribution, potentially derived from an underlying noise source. Notably, the fluctuation-ignoring approach fails to account for the probability of density reductions greater than a certain threshold in a variable density medium, which is less likely than an absolute value of zero. This fundamental point addresses a major criticism of the fluctuation-based method, a notion that has been debated in the literature for decades.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. If AI systems fail to provide the necessary explanations, users may become wary or even reject them. This crucial problem is given the term "explainability crisis" in the industry, where researchers attempt to tackle it by reducing the gap between AI systems and user understanding. This study proposes a new approach to address the explainability dilemma by first enabling AI systems to comprehend users' explanatory needs and subsequently fulfilling those needs. To achieve this, the paper offers a framework that facilitates the translation of users' explanatory demands into a viable strategy for the AI system. This framework involves treating requirements engineering techniques to categorize users' explanatory demands and using them to outline a usable interface for the AI system. A case study demonstrating the implementation of this framework in the healthcare sector is also presented. The paper's findings, which stem from an empirical analysis with healthcare professionals, indicate that this approach can effectively aid the explainability crisis by providing valuable insights for AI system development.

Our dataset, UniToPatho, has been created to contribute to the development of computational pathology methods that can accurately diagnose and evaluate colorectal polyps based on histopathological tissue samples. The dataset comprises 1597 histological images, segmented and annotated from 284 slides containing various types of colorectal epithelial lesions. Our objective is to hold a challenge to predict adenoma dysplasia grades in these images or to differentiate between benign, adenomatous, and serrated lesions. The challenge is centered around the subtasks of identifying the epithelial components of images, categorizing adenomas according to their dysplasia levels, and distinguishing between benign, adenomatous, and serrated polyps. The dataset is accessible via our website at the address: https://pitailingboard.net/unito_patho.

In a basic encoding scenario, a source with confidentiality restrictions sends data to a receiver through an unbiased channel. We're examining how the source data is encoded and the encoding scheme is constructed to prevent source leakage, which means the receiver shouldn't be able to determine any two distinct input values as their outputs. From a graph theory perspective, we can represent source encodings as graphs, where vertices are possible source values, and edges represent valid transitions between these values. We're looking for the minimal graph edges that guarantee zero error leakage for any input distribution. We're providing a simple illustration of a leakage-free encoding in binary source encoding with two-valued inputs. We're also exploring the differences and commonalities between classical binary leakage-free encoding and the general case of leakage-free encoding for sources with more than two possible values.

Deep learning-based radar image enhancement techniques have been widely adopted due to their superior performance over conventional methods. The development of a novel deep learning-based algorithm, MrSARP, for radar image enhancement is presented in this research. MrSARP is a multi-scale, deep generative model built upon a complex network of blocks for radar image enhancement, trained using synthetic data. The algorithm's primary advantage lies in its capacity to handle images of varied scales through a series of transformations at different hierarchy levels. The model's effectiveness was validated across multiple centers of gravity on an image dataset of scales 2, 4, and 8. The results show a significant improvement in the image quality following enhancement, as demonstrated by the NSS and CUI metrics in multiple frequency domains, outperforming the existing VDSR model in the process.

A novel approach called Bayesian QAOA is introduced to optimize variational quantum algorithms using quantum circuits. This method, Bayesian QAOA, determines the optimal parameters for the quantum circuit by analyzing the circuit's output on a classical computer with a Bayesian perspective. Currently, there is no theoretical justification for the widely employed maximum likelihood principle in quantum circuit training. We claim that this approach leads to overfitting due to the abundance of quantum noise. As an alternative, we suggest using the Bayesian method to search for parameter optimizations, arguing its superiority over traditional maximum likelihood optimization. Our findings, corroborated by numerical experiments, demonstrate that Bayesian QAOA generally performs better than the standard maximum likelihood approach, especially in noisy environments. This method can be found on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/QuantumBox/BayesianQAOA.

This research introduces a method to identify the areas where intersections occur between a series of ellipses. The proposed approach calculates the intersection regions between two ellipses and generalizes this operation to obtain the intersection regions of a collection of ellipses through a divide-and-conquer approach. The algorithm's time complexity is influenced by the number of intersection regions' boundaries, which in the worst-case scenario amounts to O(n) when all boundary points are calculated. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness through the computation of intersection regions for a satellite constellation depicted in a spherical projection.

A fundamental concept in real-world exploration, discovery, and learning often rely on discovering patterns within continuous datasets. However, the problem of discovering patterns in continuous data with a specific duration (being either start or end time-based) is not well-defined, especially when considering datasets with incomplete and noisy data. To address this, we've developed an approach for continuous duration data discovery, which involves mapping duration to a finite, infinite, or fractional vector space. This approach can be optimized through a non-parametric technique, which we've tested on various datasets and found to be an effective method for continuous duration data discovery. This work is part of the IJCAI 2021 Discovery Science conference.

We conducted an extensive study on the one-band Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with an adjustable interaction strength, applying a high-temperature expansion to the spirit of the Landau theory to investigate magnetic properties. Within this theoretical framework, we found that the ground state exhibits an incommensurate, stripe-like arrangement in the simple triangular lattice and a 120-degree, spiral pattern in the Kagome lattice. As the interaction increases, both systems transition into a state with magnetic oscillations as the intermediate phase. Through a detailed analysis of the magnetic free energy, we demonstrated that the magnetic oscillations emerge as the immediate outcome of the incommensurate, stripe-like arrangement becoming unstable. Furthermore, our work reveals that the 120-degree, spiral ground state becomes unstable at a certain interaction strength and converts into a state with magnetic oscillations. In contrast, the incommensurate, stripe-like arrangement remains stable at all interaction strengths in the simple triangular lattice. Additionally, we identified the magnetic oscillations as an instance of an order-by-disorder phenomenon, where quantum fluctuations favor a state with lower symmetry.

Vertebral localization and recognition are crucial processes in spinal analysis. However, due to similar appearances between adjacent vertebrae, especially in the lumbar region, it is extremely challenging to automatically identify their boundaries. To address this difficulty, researchers often employ labor-intensive and unreliable point-based methods to solve the problem. This study presents an advanced, automated system for vertebral boundary localization that relies on a unique combination of techniques. By initially correcting the spine's posture, the study eliminates side effects from lateral deformation and enhances vertebral distinguishability. Leveraging this correction, the team developed an optimization method to determine vertebral boundaries, utilizing anatomical constraints to ensure accurate and reasonable solutions. Through extensive testing on a large, public dataset with diverse cases, the proposed system achieved superior performance, outshining current state-of-the-art approaches and being robust against varying vertebral widths.

This paper is the first in a series that explores linear response in statistical mechanics and its relationship to random matrix theory's linear spectral fluctuations. We've substantiated a significant concept - that certain averages based on the steady-state probability distribution of a system remain unaffected by changes in its internal composition. This idea is proven to be true even in situations where the system experiences periodic driving forces. This notion is then applied to a statistical mechanics model and asymptotic averages are calculated for both strong and weak periodic driving forces. We've also confirmed that linear responses for both macroscopic and spectral properties follow the same pattern as observed in random matrix theory.

We use techniques from relative duality and topological field theory to establish that birational equivalences preserve the quantum numbers of the Picard-Fuchs hypergeometric equation, which serves as a marker for its cohomology. As an outcome, we show that birational equivalences maintain the topological properties of the relative quantum field that was initially defined by Cox and Schenck.

Theoretical and experimental studies have shown that there is strong, nonradiative coupling of acoustic waves between closely spaced piezoelectric materials. This finding holds true for both parallel and perpendicular orientations of the acoustic wave sources. A detailed analysis of the experiment was conducted using a geometric theory, which revealed that the primary mode of acoustic wave coupling is due to the activation of domain walls within the piezoelectric materials, allowing for efficient transmission of the signal. This mechanism may provide a basis for innovative, noncontact acoustic sensors.

We introduce a cutting-edge technique for producing large-scale aggregates of exciton-polariton bosonic lasers through the coordinated manipulation of optical resonators and spin-dependent interactions. A key innovation in our approach involves the use of sequential optical pulses in a specific sequence that creates conditions of both photon-induced spin exchange and phase-coherent output. Our findings demonstrate the production of extensive polariton clusters in a single cavity environment and the observation of their rapid expansion into multiple output cavities, featuring both thermal and Bose-Einstein condensate regimes of operation. The method also allows for the exploration of complex many-body physics via in-plane and out-of-plane optical interactions in the system.

The exoplanet, K2-22b, has been identified as a victim of periodic high-speed cosmic rain, or more precisely, it experiences episodes of intense gravitational pull every 3.05 days due to its proximity to its host star. This distinctive periodicity has enabled scientists to investigate the planet's atmospheric behavior on a shorter timescale, a pattern not typically observed in Earth's atmosphere. Our analysis of data from the Large Binocular Telescope, utilizing the Phase-Randomized Matched Filtering technique, has led to a breakthrough discovery: the planet's atmosphere is experiencing rapid mass loss due to decreased dust grain sizes. This finding presents a challenge to current dust models, suggesting that complex processes are involved in shaping the planet's atmosphere. This new evidence is expected to stimulate the development of increased computational powers, driving our understanding of planet evolution to a new level.

We establish a condition for coherence in the Milnor fiber of a complex-valued polynomial in terms of its critical set being a coherent set. Additionally, our analysis reveals specific criteria under which the critical set will be coherent, such as when the critical locus does not intersect the Milnor tube. This enumeration allows us to previously undiscovered invariant reasons for coherence in the Milnor fiber.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform engine for data analysis that's compatible with Microsoft.NET Framework and.NET Core. Designed to streamline data preparation and analysis, Daany is optimized for native.NET use. At its core are elements for linear algebra and matrix operations, but it also offers advanced statistical capabilities and fast matrix processing. The engine is particularly suitable for tasks like dimension reduction, clustering, and rapid data transformation. By leveraging Daany's API, developers can quickly perform data analysis and avoid time-consuming computations, utilizing popular.NET programming languages like C# and F#. Including detailed API guides and comprehensive unit test cases, Daany is an invaluable tool for data analysts and.NET developers.

My argument challenges the conventional view that mathematics was pivotal in the progression of the scientific revolution.  I claim, instead, that mathematics served as a byproduct of the revolution, primarily used in the later stages to legitimize and popularize key discoveries.  This claim is based on an examination of Galileo's career, suggesting that his success was fueled more by philosophical concerns than mathematical expertise.  I also consider Newton, contrasting Galileo's approach with Newton's extensive mathematical endeavors.

New research focuses on how electrons and photons interacted early in the universe's evolution, a process known as Saha's ionization. This theoretical study examines how this interaction, governed by the Saha equation, affects the universe's density in the primordial phase. To investigate these effects, the researchers developed a mathematical model based on a nonlinear problem, which revealed that the interaction could either increase or decrease the universe's density in a periodic pattern. This pattern is influenced by the universe's expansion rate and the relative number of electrons and photons. To determine whether these density changes could lead to a universe with a different matter-to-radiation balance, the researchers calculated the radiation pressure using the Einstein's algebraic state factor, which led to a significant discovery. The impacts of Saha's ionization could cause periods of rapid universe expansion, which might lead to periods of higher matter-to-radiation balance ratios. This finding is consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background's fluctuations. To further investigate these findings, the researchers analyzed the dynamics of a universe with a variable cosmological constant and identified a universe with a higher matter-to-radiation balance ratio. This research is significant because it suggests that the Saha equation's non-Gaussian impacts could have influenced the universe's evolution and may still affect its matter-to-radiation balance ratios today.

This study uses the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations to simulate the integration of two magnetic islands and observe the electromagnetic responses during their merging. An embedded Particle-In-Cellof approach is used to verify exclusive electrostatic responses. Our results reveal that when the embedded electron inertia is set to zero, the MHD simulation accurately captures the MHD-EPCI model's behavior, including their comparative statics and dynamics. However, small discrepancies arise in the simulation's early stages due to electron decoupling. By comparing the embedded electron inertia with the kinetic length, we find that electron coupling is effectively maintained when the inertia exceeds the kinetic length. Our study provides a foundation for evaluating the MHD-EPCI model's applicability in efficiently modeling complex magnetic field configurations and facilitating the development of hybrid simulations with electrostatic particle-in-cell components.

This paper introduces a novel technique to rapidly create functional code in a flow-based programming language, specifically Superfluid. This method leverages the ability of programmers to craft predictive text using sequential decision trees and allows experienced programmers to train machines to create code templates, thereby generating useful functions through a learning process. The technique is notable for requiring only a single session to develop a functional program, a feat that Programmers Inc. has verified by conducting numerous experiments. The company has even created a browser-based tool to help users train machine-generated code, which can be downloaded and executed on the Superfluid platform to produce unique videos. Programmers Inc. is now exploring ways to apply this technique to Superfluid's visual animation tools, which would enable the generation of engaging videos without requiring deep understanding of the program's logic.
